title: Newton's Third Law
learning_goal: Illustrate and analyze simultaneous forces between two objects using Newton's Third Law.

stages.title: 1. Forces come in interaction pairs
stages.content: Newton's Third Law states that when object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts an equal-magnitude force in the opposite direction on object A.

stages.title: 2. The pair acts on different objects
stages.content: Third-law forces do not cancel each other because they act on different objects. When a foot pushes backward on the ground, the ground pushes forward on the foot.

stages.title: 3. Worked example
stages.content: A swimmer pushes water backward with a force of 120 N. The water pushes the swimmer forward with a force of 120 N. The forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different objects.

stages.title: 4. Guided practice
stages.prompt: A truck pushes on a stalled car with 800 N. What force does the car exert on the truck?
stages.hint: Third-law force pairs always have equal magnitude and opposite direction.
stages.alternate_explanation: Name the interaction both ways: truck on car, then car on truck.

stages.title: 5. Avoid a common mistake
stages.content: The larger or heavier object does not exert a larger third-law force. The interaction forces are always equal in magnitude, even though the two objects may accelerate differently because their masses differ.

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, identify action-reaction pairs, state which object each force acts on, compare force magnitudes, and explain why the paired forces do not cancel.

concept_cards.title: Name the interaction both ways
concept_cards.content: If A exerts a force on B, B simultaneously exerts an equal-magnitude opposite-direction force on A. Write “A on B” and “B on A” to identify the pair. These are forces of the same interaction type.

concept_cards.title: Separate the objects
concept_cards.content: Third-law forces act on different objects. They cannot cancel in the net force on a single object. When both objects belong to a larger system, the pair is internal to that system and cancels in the system force sum.

concept_cards.title: Equal forces do not imply equal accelerations
concept_cards.content: Use a = F_net/m for each object separately. A light car and heavy truck exert equal contact forces on each other, but their accelerations need not be equal. Compare net forces as well as masses.

concept_cards.title: Balanced forces are a different relationship
concept_cards.content: Weight and normal force can balance on a resting book, but both act on the book. The third-law partner of Earth’s force on the book is the book’s force on Earth, not the table’s normal force.

conceptual_questions.prompt: During a collision, why can the small car accelerate more even though its contact force equals the truck’s?
expected_ideas: Third-law interaction forces have equal magnitudes.
Acceleration depends on net force and mass; with comparable net force, smaller mass means larger acceleration.
misconceptions: Greater damage proves a larger interaction force.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: How does each mass enter a = F_net/m?

conceptual_questions.prompt: Explain why a rocket can accelerate in a vacuum.
expected_ideas: The rocket pushes expelled gas backward.
The gas exerts a simultaneous forward force on the rocket; air is unnecessary.
misconceptions: A rocket must push on surrounding air.
